title: identity and first repo
goal: A1 A repository, an identity, and one commit you made on purpose
startWith: Open a terminal in an empty folder. Everything in this stage happens in a throwaway repo called git-lab — you will rewrite its history later, so do not use real work.

newIdeas.plain: A folder with a .git directory. All history lives there; delete it and you have plain files again.
A snapshot of the whole tree plus who, when and why, identified by a hash.
Three places a change can be: edited on disk, staged for the next commit, already committed.

tasks.do: Set your name and email globally, and check what git already thinks they are
tasks.why: Every commit records them permanently. Fixing them later means rewriting history.
tasks.how: Set them once per machine; a repo-local override drops the --global.

blocks.label: terminal
blocks.body:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --list --show-origin | grep -E 'user\.|init\.'

blocks.label: IntelliJ
blocks.body: Settings → Version Control → Git has no identity field — IntelliJ reads this same global config. Set it in the terminal once and every IDE commit uses it.

tasks.do: Create the lab repo and make the first commit
tasks.why: init then add then commit is the whole model in three commands.

blocks.label: terminal
blocks.body:
mkdir git-lab && cd git-lab
git init
echo '# git lab' > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "first commit"

blocks.label: IntelliJ
blocks.body: VCS → Enable Version Control Integration creates the repo. New files raise a dialog asking to add them — that dialog is git add.

tasks.do: Look at the same commit three ways: status, log, show
tasks.why: Most git confusion is not knowing which of the three areas a change is sitting in. These three answer that.

blocks.label: terminal
blocks.body:
git status -sb
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
git show --stat HEAD

blocks.label: IntelliJ
blocks.body: The Git tool window (Alt+9) is the same three views: Commit tab is status, Log tab is log, clicking a commit is show.

tasks.do: Stage a change, then unstage it without losing the edit
tasks.why: Staging is a decision you can take back. Knowing that is what makes small commits cheap.

blocks.label: terminal
blocks.body:
echo 'line two' >> README.md
git add README.md
git status -s          # M in the left column = staged
git restore --staged README.md
git status -s          # M moved right: unstaged, edit intact

check.run: # read the two status lines: the M changes column and the edit survives
check.expect: the M moves from left to right

tasks.do: Write a commit message a stranger can act on
tasks.why: A subject is read in a log of 500; the body is read by whoever debugs your change at 3am.
tasks.how: Imperative subject under 50 characters, blank line, then why — not what, the diff already says what.

blocks.label: terminal
blocks.body:
git add -A
git commit             # opens your editor: subject, blank line, body

blocks.label: IntelliJ
blocks.body: Ctrl+K opens the Commit dialog. The message box is the same thing; the checkbox list on the left is the index.

proof.note: Commits in a repo you created, with messages you meant.

doneWhen: You can say, for any file, whether it is untracked, modified, staged or committed — without guessing.

lessons.title: The Git tool window (Alt+9)
lessons.teach: Alt+9 opens Git. Two tabs matter: Commit is git status with checkboxes, Log is git log --graph you can click. Everything in stage A has a home in here.
lessons.fallbackTip: Older builds call it Version Control; newer ones split Commit into its own tool window.

lessons.title: Commit without the terminal (Ctrl+K)
lessons.teach: Ctrl+K. The checkbox list is the index — ticking a file is git add, and unticking it is git restore --staged. The diff on the right is what you are about to commit, so read it before you write the message.
